title: Why There Aren't So Many Hotel Fires Anymore
summary: Josh and Chuck examine a cluster of deadly hotel fires in 1946, focusing on the LaSalle Hotel fire in Chicago (June 5), the Hotel Canfield fire in Dubuque, Iowa (June 19), and the Baker Hotel gas explosion in Dallas (June 21), then the Winecoff Hotel fire in Atlanta (December 7, 1946), the deadliest hotel fire in US history with 119 deaths. They cover the flammable interiors, open transoms and fire doors, the lack of alarms and sprinklers, escape attempts, the famous Arnold Hardy photo of Daisy Mccomber, and how the fires led to local fire code reforms (sprinklers, closed fire doors, banned transoms, mandatory fire escapes, and retroactive application to existing hotels). They also discuss the 1980 MGM Grand fire, alarm levels in firefighting, and a listener mail about Monica Seles being stabbed and related security changes in tennis.

segments.title: Opening banter and why hotel fires
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic of hotel fires, mention the MGM Grand fire, and note how flammable materials and lack of regulation made older buildings dangerous.

segments.title: LaSalle Hotel fire, Chicago 1946
segments.summary: A June 1946 fire at Chicago's LaSalle Hotel started in a cardboard box of cigarette butts behind the Silver Grill cocktail lounge. A fifteen-minute delay in calling the fire department, open transoms, propped fire doors, and a ventilation shaft let it spread fast. A switchboard operator stayed on the line calling rooms and died; sixty-one people died in total.

segments.title: Hotel Canfield fire, Dubuque, and Baker Hotel explosion, Dallas
segments.summary: Two weeks after Chicago, a fire started in a cigarette dumping closet at the Hotel Canfield in Dubuque, Iowa, killing nineteen. Days later, a gas explosion at Dallas's Baker Hotel killed ten. Three June fires in 1946 killed about ninety people and drew national attention.

segments.title: Winecoff Hotel fire, Atlanta, December 1946
segments.summary: The Winecoff Hotel in Atlanta, a fifteen-story building with no sprinklers, alarms, fire doors, or fire escapes, caught fire around 3 a.m. on December 7, 1946. The cause is disputed: a deliberate mattress fire theory versus a careless cigarette or accelerant. The central stairwell around the elevator shaft carried smoke upward, trapping guests on upper floors.

segments.title: Escapes and casualties at the Winecoff
segments.summary: Guests jumped, tied bed sheets, or tried to reach nets and adjacent buildings. Jimmy Cahill bridged a gap with scaffolding to rescue his mother. The death toll was 119, including 39 people under twenty.

segments.title: Reforms: fire codes, sprinklers, transoms, and fire escapes
segments.summary: The fires led local governments to adopt codes requiring sprinklers, alarms, closed fire doors, banned transoms, mandatory fire escapes, and retroactive application to existing hotels. President Truman called a national conference on fire prevention. The 1980 MGM Grand fire happened because sprinklers had not been installed. The hosts discuss open-plan offices.

segments.title: Arnold Hardy photo and fire alarm levels
segments.summary: Arnold Hardy's photo of Daisy Mccomber falling from the Winecoff won a Pulitzer Prize. Hardy kicked in a drugstore door to get supplies and paid for it. The hosts explain that fire alarm levels indicate the number of units dispatched and that the Winecoff fire escalated to four alarms.

segments.title: Listener mail: Monica Seles stabbing and tennis security
segments.summary: A listener from Topeka, Kansas notes that Monica Seles was stabbed courtside by a Steffi Graf fan, that her loud shriek drew complaints, and that tennis tours increased security, with guards now standing behind players during changeovers.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh thanks the listener and gives contact information for the show.
